messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Paramedic
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 35

# Vignette: Rajan

Rajan is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has spent the better part of four decades working as a paramedic. He is the kind of man who takes quiet pride in his steadiness — colleagues have long described him as unflappable, the one you want beside you when everything is falling apart. His wife, Priya, says he has always been like that, calm in a way that made her feel safe. That steadiness is part of what makes the past two years so disorienting for him. He is no longer sure he recognizes himself.

Two years ago, Rajan and his crew responded to an industrial call at a chemical processing facility on the outskirts of the city. There had been a leak — the details were confused on dispatch, as they often are. What he walked into was not what he had been told to expect. Several workers were down, and the air had a quality he still cannot quite describe, something sharp and wrong that he felt in the back of his throat before he understood what was happening. He and a colleague worked for nearly twenty minutes in that environment before proper hazmat support arrived and they were pulled out. In the days that followed, Rajan experienced burning in his airways, headaches, and a fatigue that felt cellular, as though something had been altered at a level he could not see. Medical assessments were inconclusive. He was told he would probably be fine.

He returned to work after a few weeks. For a while, things seemed manageable. Then, gradually, they were not.

The smell is what catches him most often — certain cleaning products, exhaust fumes, even the antiseptic inside the ambulance bay can stop him cold. His chest tightens and his mind goes somewhere he does not want it to go, back to the floor of that facility, back to the particular quality of that air. He does not panic in the way people might imagine. It is quieter than that, and in some ways worse — a sudden, absolute certainty that something is wrong with his body, that whatever entered him that day is still there, still working. He finds himself monitoring his breathing throughout a shift, cataloguing sensations, wondering whether a headache is ordinary or something more. At night he sleeps poorly, and when he does sleep he sometimes wakes with his heart going fast, though he rarely remembers a specific dream.

He has pulled back from his crew in ways he does not fully acknowledge. He takes on more paperwork-heavy roles when he can. He tells himself this is appropriate for a man his age, that younger paramedics should be running the difficult calls. Priya has noticed that he is more irritable at home, quicker to withdraw after a long shift. He knows she is watching him with a particular kind of attention and he finds it both comforting and unbearable. He does not want to be watched.

What troubles him most, when he allows himself to sit with it, is the loss of something he cannot name precisely. He used to feel competent in his body — forty years of physically demanding work had given him a trust in himself that was almost unconscious. That trust is gone. He is hyperaware of his physical sensations in a way that exhausts him, and he carries a low-grade dread about his long-term health that no reassurance has been able to fully quiet. He wonders what the chemicals did that the tests could not find.

He came to therapy at Priya's urging, and he was clear in the first session that he was not someone who talked about himself easily. He is precise and thoughtful when he does speak, choosing his words carefully. He says he does not understand why he cannot simply move forward. He has seen far worse in his career. He says this as though it is an argument he is losing.
